ch02.note: Fourth Avenue (四马路), today Fuzhou Road, was a street of the International Settlement famous for its bookshops, teahouses, theaters and newspaper offices, and notorious for its brothels; the produce market of these opening scenes stood along it.

The Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局) governed the foreign-run International Settlement, and its own force, the Municipal Police, policed it. Because the Nationalists' Longhua garrison had no lawful power to make arrests inside the Settlement, it had to work through the Council's police; that jurisdictional seam runs through the whole of the arrest.

Cuckoo Soul Abroad (海外鹃魂) was an early 1930s film of the Lianhua company; its star Jin Yan (金焰), a Korea-born actor hailed as the 'Emperor of Film,' played opposite the actress Ziluolan. In classical verse the cuckoo (杜鹃) is said to weep blood for grief, which sharpens Wei Dafu's joke that all three leads end up dead. (Corroborated.)

Longhua (龙华), southwest of the city, was the seat of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison Command and its prison, beside the Longhua Temple and its ancient pagoda. In February 1931 the Nationalists secretly shot some two dozen Communists here—the 'Longhua Martyrs,' among them the 'Five Martyrs' of the League of Left-Wing Writers (Rou Shi, Hu Yepin, Yin Fu, Feng Keng and Li Weisen), a killing mourned by Lu Xun. It is to this garrison that the prisoners of the novel are taken. (Corroborated.)

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (招商局), founded by the Qing statesman Li Hongzhang (here 'Grand Secretary Li'), was at the center of a real 1933 scandal. Li's grandson Li Guojie (李国杰), who ran one of its arms, was accused of mortgaging the company's Shanghai wharves—among them the Jinliyuan of the earlier scene—for a vast loan to an American shipping firm and pocketing the kickback, with Chen Fumu (陈孚木) as a go-between; a Shanghai court sentenced Li to eight years in April 1933, and Chen fled. The gangster Du Yuesheng (the 'tycoon Du') and the Hatchet Gang's earlier killing of the company's Nanjing-appointed director hover behind the affair as the detectives gossip it. (Corroborated.)

ch03.note: The Central Party Affairs Investigation Section (党务调查科) was the Kuomintang's political-intelligence organ, run under the Central Organization Department by the Chen brothers' faction and later by Xu Enzeng; those in the know called its Nanjing base, in the Zhanyuan garden, the 'Special Operations Headquarters.' It was the forerunner of the wartime Bureau of Investigation and Statistics (中统). You Tianxiao's secret post in it, outranking his open one, is the source of his double-dealing. (Corroborated.)

Xi Shi (西施), a legendary beauty of the state of Yue in the Spring and Autumn era, was by tradition sent to beguile the king of rival Wu and hasten its ruin—the archetypal planted agent. As a cryptonym for a mole inside the enemy's ranks it is pointed; the identity of 'Xi Shi' is one of the book's central secrets.

ch04.anchor: Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic
ch04.note: The Emergency Law for Crimes Endangering the Republic (危害民国紧急治罪法), promulgated by the Nationalist government in 1931, prescribed death for a range of acts against the state and was the chief legal instrument used against Communists; hence the interrogator's threat of the firing squad. (Corroborated.)

Haohan (浩瀚, 'the vast') is the working alias of a senior Communist the enemy is hunting; within the Party he was known for articles published under the name in The Guide Weekly (向导), the Central Committee's organ of the 1920s. His whereabouts, and who among the arrested may be his contact, are the engine of the plot.

The May Thirtieth Movement (五卅运动) was the wave of anti-imperialist strikes and protests that swept China after Settlement police shot Chinese demonstrators in Shanghai on 30 May 1925; it drew many, like Ling Wen and her husband, into the revolution. The Northern Expedition she goes on to mention set out from Guangzhou in 1926; the Nationalist purge of Communists began in 1927. (Corroborated.)

ch05.note: Da Hong Pao (大红袍, 'Great Red Robe') is the most storied of the Wuyi 'rock teas,' a heavily oxidized oolong grown on the cliffs of Mount Wuyi in Fujian and long counted among the most prized teas in China.

The Nineteenth Route Army (十九路军) was the Cantonese force that put up fierce resistance to the Japanese at Shanghai in the 'January 28' Incident of 1932 (一·二八, the first Battle of Shanghai); it was afterwards sent to fight Communists in Fujian. 'Commander Cai' is the army's general Cai Tingkai. (Corroborated.)

Xuanwu Lake (玄武湖) lies against the northeastern wall of Nanjing; the drive in this chapter runs beside its stretch of the great Ming-dynasty city wall, past Jiming Temple (鸡鸣寺) and out by the Shence Gate (神策门). Nanjing was the Nationalist capital and the seat of the secret-service headquarters to which You Tianxiao reports.
